deep.reconstruction:
The right-hand page (fol. 75) holds four separate jottings. Two are slips pasted over older text. The visible left-margin fragments ('...che Integral für die', '...dass die ζ Function', '...die Höhe (Geschlecht)', 's = 1/2', 'const. s l(s)') are the edge of the facing page, transcribed separately as the previous page. That page shows ξ(s) has genus 1 in t² without Riemann's integral.

(1) Research programme: 'Determine all number fields, of any degree, with discriminant 2, 3, 4, 5.' In modern terms: classify K/Q with |d_K| ≤ 5.
- Minkowski's bound |d_K| ≥ (π/4)^n (n^n/n!)^2 grows with n, so it bounds the degree. Hermite's theorem then gives finiteness.
- The answer is: none with |d| = 2; Q(√−3) for 3; Q(i) for 4; Q(√5) for 5. Degrees ≥ 3 already need |d| ≥ 23.
- Hilbert states this only as a task and does no computation.

(2) Remark on lemniscatic complex multiplication. In Z[i] one should also admit 'powers' (a+bi)^{k+ih} with Gaussian-integer exponents. These are not ordinary powers: they are realised by lemniscatic functions, since sl(μu) is a rational function of sl(u) for μ ∈ Z[i]. Hilbert says that modulo 1+i the same simple addition theorem holds as for the exponential function. This is the Gaussian analogue of the exponential/cyclotomic situation (Abel, Eisenstein, Kronecker). The next page develops it into the programme that became Hilbert's 12th problem: functions that belong to an arbitrary number field as exp belongs to Q.

(3) Reference: Jacobi, Werke Bd. 2, S. 85, with the remark that modular functions are algebraic functions of functions of one variable. Bibliographic only.

(4) Main derivation (pasted slip): the complementary ideal of an ideal A is (AD)^{-1}, D the different.

Setup:
- Let K have degree n, ring of integers O with basis ω_1..ω_n, and discriminant d.
- Put Ω = det(ω_j^{(i)}), so Ω² = d.
- Let Ω_1..Ω_n be the cofactors of Ω along the first conjugate row.
- Let A have Z-basis τ_1..τ_n, T = det(τ_j^{(i)}), and T_1..T_n the corresponding first minors.

Step a [my gloss]. By Cramer's rule, T_j/T = τ_j^{*} is the trace-dual basis: Tr(τ_i τ_j^{*}) = δ_ij, so T_j/T ∈ K. Since T² = N(A)² d is rational, T·T_j = T² τ_j^{*} ∈ K. Hilbert asserts that T T_1, ..., T T_n is a basis of an ideal J. He defines A_0 := T²/J; the goal is A_0 = AD. Equivalently, (T_1..T_n) = J/T = T/A_0.

Step b. Choose α with α ≡ 0 (mod AJ); the transcription '=' should probably read '≡ 0'. Choose β ∈ J coprime to N(α) and to D. Look at a first minor of T, an (n−1)×(n−1) determinant of conjugates. Multiply its conjugate rows by β^{(i)}/α^{(i)}, which turns the entries into integers. The resulting determinant is divisible by the corresponding minor Ω_n of the integral-basis matrix. Hence (β'β''…/α'α''…)·J is divisible by T(Ω_1..Ω_n). Hence Aβ'β''…J is divisible by N(A) T (Ω_1..Ω_n). Hence, removing the factor β'β''…, which is coprime to the relevant ideals, A(T_1..T_n) is divisible by N(A)(Ω_1..Ω_n).

Step c. Both sides have the same norm. Using T = ±N(A)Ω, the norm of the left side is N(A)·N(T)/N(A_0) and of the right side N(A)^n N(Ω)/N(D). So divisibility becomes equality: A(T_1..T_n) = N(A)(Ω_1..Ω_n).

Step d. By the case A = O, (Ω_1..Ω_n) = Ω/D; this is Dedekind's theorem that the complementary module of O is D^{-1}. Hence A·T/A_0 = N(A)Ω/D. With T = N(A)Ω this gives A_0 = AD. Equivalently, the dual basis of A spans (AD)^{-1}.

Step e. Hilbert notes that for algebraic functions this theorem contains the Riemann–Roch theorem, citing Landsberg in the Göttinger Nachrichten (c. 1897–98). The dual of a divisor's module, twisted by the different/canonical class, is the Riemann–Roch duality.
errors: The ideal (T T_1, ..., T T_n) and the minors T_j involve all conjugates, so they lie in the Galois closure, not in K. The ideal-theoretic manipulations, including 'divisible by T', are carried out formally in a larger field without comment. Only T_j/T and T T_j lie in K; this is unstated.
The definition of α is garbled: 'α = AJ' cannot be literal, since AJ is an ideal. It must mean α ≡ 0 (mod AJ) or α a number of AJ chosen to clear denominators.
The minor written as T_n uses rows ' and '' and columns τ_1..τ_{n−1}. Cofactors of first-row entries should omit the first conjugate row, so the indexing is loose.

The step from 'Aβ'β''…J divisible by N(A)T(Ω)' to 'A(T_1..T_n) divisible by N(A)(Ω)' silently uses that the norm of β is coprime to the ideals involved; that is why β was chosen prime to N(α) and D. The step is a sketch, not a full proof.
The base case (Ω_1..Ω_n) = Ω/D, i.e. Dedekind's complementary-module theorem, is used without proof here.
Sign: T = ±N(A)Ω. This is harmless for ideals.

results.what: Programme: list all number fields with |discriminant| ∈ {2,3,4,5}
results.modern_name: Classification of number fields of small discriminant (Minkowski bound, Hermite finiteness)

results.what: Gaussian-integer 'powers' via lemniscatic functions; an addition theorem mod 1+i analogous to the exponential
results.modern_name: Complex multiplication of the lemniscatic curve; Lubin–Tate-type analogue of exp for Q(i); Kronecker's Jugendtraum / Hilbert's 12th problem
results.usually_credited_to: Abel, Eisenstein (lemniscatic CM); Kronecker; Hilbert (12th problem, 1900); Lubin–Tate (1965) for the formal-group analogue

results.what: The dual (complementary) basis of an ideal A, given by the cofactors T_j/T of the conjugate matrix, spans (AD)^{-1}; equivalently A_0 = T²/J = AD
results.modern_name: Complementary module / inverse different: A* = A^{-1} D^{-1}
results.usually_credited_to: Dedekind (1882, Über die Discriminanten endlicher Körper; Supplement XI); also in Hilbert's Zahlbericht (1897)

results.what: The analogy that this duality contains Riemann–Roch for algebraic functions
results.modern_name: Arithmetic analogue of Riemann–Roch via the different / Serre duality via trace

deep.surprise_reason: The ideal-theoretic proof is Dedekind's complementary-module theorem in Hilbert's determinantal style; the Riemann–Roch remark explicitly credits Landsberg. The small-discriminant task is a programme note. The lemniscatic 'powers' remark is an early private trace of Hilbert's 12th-problem programme. It is interesting but consistent with what is known of his interests.

checkable.asserts: For Z[i] with basis 1,i, Ω² = d = −4.
The dual basis (cofactors/Ω) of {1,i} is {1/2, −i/2} in both embeddings. It spans (1/2)Z[i] = D^{-1}, with D = (2) the different of Q(i).
For A = (1+i) with Z-basis 1+i, 2: T² = N(A)² d = 4·(−4), i.e. T = ±N(A)Ω.
The first dual-basis element of A=(1+i) times (1+i)·2 is integral (here 1−i), consistent with A* = (A·D)^{-1} = ((1+i)·2)^{-1}Z[i].

checkable.sympy: discriminant(x**2+x+1, x) == -3 and discriminant(x**2+1, x) == -4 and discriminant(x**2-x-1, x) == 5

checkable.asserts: No quadratic field has |d| = 2: fundamental discriminants are ≡ 0,1 mod 4 and 2 is not.
The Minkowski lower bounds for |d| are about 1.23 (n=2) and 3.13 (n=3). The minimum actually attained for cubics is 23 > 5, so only quadratic fields occur.

transcription_corrections: 'Lemniscatenfunctionen' and 'Exponentialfunction' are confirmed by the image. The phrase 'für die Exponentialfunction' is underlined.
The Jacobi line reads roughly 'Jacobi Werke Bd. 2 S. 85 Bemerkung dass die Modul-Functionen algebr. Fctn. von Functionen einer Variabeln sind'. 'einer' is underlined.
'Es sei α = AJ' is likely 'α ≡ 0 (AJ)' or a number α of AJ; the image is ambiguous.
The left-margin fragments ('...che Integral für die', etc.) belong to the facing verso/previous page, not to fol. 75.
In 'so [-...-] sind (TT_1,...)' the deleted word is probably 'wird'. The deleted symbol before T²/J resembles a crossed-out fraction or J.
